utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I wish to greet the Prosecutor and the Defence. Hello, ladies and gentlemen. Also, I say hello to the technical booth and the interpreters. Is everyone ready to start? However, before we start, we must say that we are here today to continue this case. Mr. Dubuisson, could you please state the number of the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-14/1-T, Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Erasmus. While I am on my feet, I am involved in another matter at the moment and may I seek Your Honours leave to attend that court during the course of the opening address. I regret very much not being able to hear the opening address by Mr. Mikulicic, but unfortunately, I am involved in this other matter for this afternoon. If I may have permission to absent myself, I would be much grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It is a pity not to be able to have you here with us, Mr. Niemann, because you certainly enrich our trial, but, of course, we do agree, and you do have leave to leave the trial. Could I have the appearance for the Defence, please, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, good morning, esteemed colleagues, Goran Mikulicic appears for the Defence and my colleague, Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In order to organise our proceedings -- thank you, Mr. Niemann -- our proceedings this afternoon, I wish to say that we would have to see how we will be working. We will be having two 20-minute breaks this afternoon. The first break would be around ten minutes to 4.00, that is to say, 15.50, and the break after that would be around twenty past 5.00. That is to say, two 20-minute breaks because for all of us who are working here, it is very important; we often forget that in the booths, there are people who are working for us, working very hard, quite often. Also, we have realised that we have assessed our efforts, and we realise that we always have interpreters with us and we always have to bear this in mind. After these pleasant words, we can start the proceedings now. I shall now give the floor to Mr. Mikulicic. You have the floor, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In our proceedings, we have come to a stage when the Defence starts presenting its case. I shall avail myself of the opportunity offered by the provisions of the Statute to make my opening statement so that I could inform the distinguished Trial Chamber of the views of the Defence with regard to this trial and also what our intentions are with regard to the rest of the case. May I just say quite briefly, without taking up too much of our time, that I think that we should recall briefly the charges that are brought against our client, Mr. Aleksovski, and then briefly we are going to recall what the Prosecutor said in his opening statement, and after that, I shall present an outline of the views of the Defence with regard to this trial and what the Defence wishes to do in this connection. The indictment has brought charges against our client in terms of three acts, Counts 8, 9, and 10. Count 8, a grave breach of the Geneva Convention from 1949, as recognised by Article 2B of the statute, so that is inhuman treatment. Count 9 of the indictment brings charges against our Defendant also in terms of a grave breach of the Geneva Convention 1949 as recognised by Article 2C of the Statute, namely, wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health. Count 10 of the indictment brings charges against our Defendant in terms of a violation of the laws or customs of war, outrages upon the personal dignity as recognised by Article 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal as well as 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. He is being charged either as the immediate perpetrator of these incriminations or as the responsible person in the chain of command. So our Defendant is charged with unlawful treatment of Bosnian Muslim detainees from the beginning of January until the end of May 1993. That is to say, that the indictment thus sets the venue of these alleged illegal acts; also, the area, and the area has thus been determined earlier in the previous proceedings through what the Trial Chamber has ruled on on the 25th of September, 1997; namely, that the area where these illegal acts were committed is Kaonik in the Municipality of Busovaca, so now we have recalled the incriminations from the indictment. The Prosecutor, as he opened his case, in his introductory statement, said that these crimes were committed in the prison of Kaonik in the Lasva Valley in a situation of an open conflict between the forces of the HVO, that is to say the military forces of the Croatian Defence Council which were allegedly assisted by the regular army of the Republic of Croatia on the one hand and, on the other hand, according to the introductory statement made by the Prosecutor, the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina also took part. Implicitly in the opening statement the Prosecutor speaks of an armed conflict with the elements of an international conflict and has charged the Defendant of being the commander of the prison in Kaonik, and that this prison was organised for detaining Muslims from the nearby villages. So this is unlawful treatment of the Bosnian Muslim detainees. The Prosecutor alleges that these civilians were detained unlawfully, that they were beaten in Kaonik, that they were tortured in Kaonik, that they were exhausted psychologically by intensive interrogations, that they were used to dig trenches and as a human shield. The Prosecutor implies that all of this happened in the area of the Lasva valley in a situation when the army of the Croatian Defence Council attacked the Muslim population. The Prosecutor believes that the Defendant, personally or in cooperation with others, planned, instigated, abetted, or otherwise assisted the commission of these unlawful acts, and that he did this either personally or by omitting to commit certain acts, by which he would punish the direct perpetrators. So this is delictum commisivum and delictum ommisivum, that is to say, the omission of commission or non-commission. In his opening statement, the Prosecutor recalled certain precedents, especially the Yamashita case and the hostages case, for which he believes that they would be applicable to this case too, which is being tried in this courtroom. The Prosecutor also implies that the Muslim civilians were detained only because of their ethnicity, because of their ethnic background, with a view to exchanges and the Defendant knew all of this, allowed this, and even planned this. Furthermore, the Prosecutor implies that the detainees were held in crowded rooms, that they had inadequate medical facilities, that they were inadequately fed, and that they were psychologically and physically mistreated. Also, the Prosecutor implies that Zlatko Aleksovski, as the commander of Kaonik, did not take necessary measures to prevent these crimes, to prohibit them, or to punish their commission, or also that he personally took part in their commission. The Prosecutor also invoked the decision of the Chamber of Appeals in the Tadic case which says that all victims should be treated alike and that the conflict in the former Yugoslavia had the character of an international conflict. The Prosecutor also invoked the Nicaragua case in which he says that as far as international conflicts are concerned, that there should be effective control over the army that is in conflict by another state. That is what the Prosecutor has highlighted in his opening statement. That is, that he will prove this or, rather, that he has proven this in his case. In contrast, at this point in time, the Defence does not wish to evaluate the Prosecutor's case because we will do this at the end of presenting our case, but may I say quite briefly that the Defence believes that in the Prosecutor's case, the international nature of the conflict was not proven at the place and in the time which is incriminated in the indictment, that is to say, in the period from the 1st of January until the 31st of May, 1993, in the area of Busovaca or, more precisely, the Kaonik facility. The Defence believes and, if we apply the standard from the Nicaragua case, this has not been proven so far, namely, that there was effective control of the Republic of Croatia over the military formations of the Croatian Defence council in the area to which the indictment pertains. We, the Defence, are going to invoke the ruling of the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case in which the Trial Chamber ruled that an international conflict has to be proven in proceedings at the time and in the place that is covered by the indictment. The Defence believes that the military command responsibility of Zlatko Aleksovski has not been proven in the hierarchy of the Croatian Defence Council in view of his military position and also that it has not been proven that he had effective control over soldiers of the Croatian Defence Council. We also believe that it has not been proven in this case that these are systematic and unlawful acts against the Muslim population. Also, that it was not proven that on any occasion Zlatko Aleksovski, either alone or in concert with other persons, planned, instigated, or ordered unlawful acts because it has not been established that he was a member of any military or politically relevant body at the critical time and in the place to which the indictment refers. Also, we believe that it has not been objectively proven that in the period covered by the indictment in the Kaonik facility, any one of the persons interned suffered great bodily injury or was killed. Such a person has never been identified and no medical documents have been offered or any other material proof which would show that there was serious deterioration of health or of the physical integrity of the said person. As the Defence views this case, in our part of the case, we shall prove as we call upon a witness, an expert for this area, that at the time and place to which the indictment refers, that is to say, Kaonik Busovaca to the first part of 1993, there were no elements of an international conflict between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. The Defence shall furthermore prove that Zlatko Aleksovski did not have effective control, in terms of command responsibility, over the HVO soldiers in view of possible excessive acts that the members of the HVO might have committed. The Defence shall also prove that Zlatko Aleksovski personally neither planned nor instigated nor ordered unlawful acts, and the Defence shall also prove that, on the other hand, with regard to certain excessive events, he did react by punishing the perpetrators within the possibilities he had, holding the position he had. The Defence shall prove that certain incidents, even if they did occur within the Kaonik facility, were the consequence of exceptional acts of irresponsible individuals, not a consequence of systematic behaviour towards the detained persons. Especially not in terms of treating the detainees in such a way because they were of Muslim origin. The Defence will also prove that the civilians were temporarily detained in Kaonik, from the Lasva Valley, and that this was done due to security reasons and in no way because persons of Muslim ethnic background were being persecuted or that their intention was to have them exchanged for Croat persons. Defence will prove the legal basis for labour done by the internees, and it will point to the essential use of Additional Protocol 2 of the Geneva Convention. The Defence will prove that the interned persons were given adequate medical care, that hygienic conditions at the Kaonik facility were in accordance with the standards of the time and space where these events took place. We mustn't forget that this is an undeveloped area, this is a time when there was armed conflict, that this is an area which was in a military environment so that some contacts for supplies from other parts of the country were not possible. In such circumstances, the Defence will determine that the conditions were of the standard that was the only one possible in that region and at that time. The Defence will also indicate that the accommodation in the Kaonik prison was in accordance with what was objectively possible, and it will point to the temporary nature of this situation, as opposed to the thesis of the long-term -- long-lasting situation. Also, the Defence will prove that the food made available to the interned persons was, in the given circumstances, adequate and at the same level that the food was organised for all people from that region at that time period. As opposed to the claims by the Prosecution that Kaonik was built for the purposes of persecution and internment of the Muslim population, the Defence will prove that this facility was not built or intended for that purpose but that due to the circumstances which were not foreseeable, but did happen at the critical time, it was simply in the absence of any other facility that this facility was used for temporary internment. The Defence will further prove that in the circumstances of armed conflict between HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, military units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked the Lasva Valley and not the other way around; that military units of the HVO attacked the Muslim population in the Lasva Valley. The Defence will further prove that in this case, the precedent from the Yamashita and the hostages cases cannot be applied and also it is not possible to apply the analogy of military command, of a military commander to Zlatko Aleksovski as the warden of the Kaonik facility as far as his command responsibility is concerned as it's incriminated by the indictment. The Defence will show you that in spite of the fact that at the given time at the Kaonik facility, there were hundreds of people temporarily interned. Nobody at the Kaonik facility was killed, nobody was seriously injured physically, or in any other way was seriously mistreated which would have the consequence of a grave harm to the health. Not one of these persons got sick from a serious illness, and none of those people who were temporarily interned at Kaonik was after being released from Kaonik was treated in hospital or as an outpatient. The place where these alleged events took place has been determined in time and space to the facility of Kaonik, as I said earlier in my decision of the 25th of September, '89. For the purpose of what I have said just now, the Defence will bring before the Trial Chamber about 20 witnesses from whom the Defence intends to have two expert witnesses, one has been announced for today and for the next few days, and the second expert witness, the Defence plans for him to speak on this case on the topic of the component of the international conflict at the end of the Defence's part of the trial. The Defence will also bring out facts through the testimony of the witnesses by which it intends to prove what I have just said. This is all that I wanted to say in my opening statement, more or less. I wouldn't wish to abuse the time available further, so that if Your Honours agree, we could start right away with the expert witness of the Defence and I will announce him when he is brought into the courtroom, so would the usher please bring in the Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, we agree, Mr. Mikulicic. Please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good day. Would you please read the oath which is written on the piece of paper? Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Could you please tell me your first name and your last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Bilandzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please, would you sit down? Thank you for coming to testify before the court. You will now respond to questions that Mr. Mikulicic, the Defence for the Defendant will ask, I think you know Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good day once again, Professor Bilandzic. Thank you for the Defence coming to, based on your expert knowledge to try, to this Trial Chamber and for all of us, to put more light on a problem that is very important in these proceedings. In order to acquaint the Trial Chamber, Professor, you are, by your qualifications, what is your area of speciality? Would you please tell us all about your career, starting from your professorship at the Faculty of Political Sciences dating from the sixties and seventies and then on until your membership at the Academy of Arts and Sciences of the Republic of Croatia. Professor, you, as a student, you completed the Franciscan gymnasium school for priests; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you finished high school and then World War II broke out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a young person, you joined the fighting in World War II and you took part in the fighting against the occupation of fascist forces on the territory of former Yugoslavia; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From the very first day of the uprising until the end?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the end of the war, participating in the military operations, you got some -- you got some military ranks.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I came out of the war as a major and I left the JNA as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Up until what year was your military career? When did you leave the army and decided to work in the civilian service?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I left the chief -- the headquarters of the JNA at the end of March in 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that, you were a professor at the Military Academy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I taught the history of the Second World War and the partisan war in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then your political engagement in the territory of former Yugoslavia came about, you became a representative -- a Croatian representative in the federal political organisations; would you tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I worked in the federal administration as a representative of Croatia, first of all in the Central Committee of the trade unions of Yugoslavia, and then a director of the Research Institute of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, of the Communist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the period of 67 to 69, you were the director of the Croatian Institute for the history of the labour movement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you became the director of the Institute for Social Research of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you devoted yourself to teaching where you remain until the present time, so from 1974 until today at the Faculty of Political Sciences?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same faculty, I was teaching from '67 to '74, so that practically I was at the faculty from '67 until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the period from '74 to '78, you were also the Dean of the Faculty of Political Sciences?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, in the meantime, you were also a member of Parliament of the Republic of Croatia, also you were a member of the central committee of the League of Communists of the Republic of Croatia, and in the period after democratic elections in the Republic of Croatia in 1990, you became Vice-President of the Republic of Croatia at the time that that post existed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now you're a member of the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences as the highest scientific body in the region of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've written many articles, many books. What is the topic, what is the scientific area that you are interested in, that you work in?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I've written eleven books out of which the most important one is the “History of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." The other works concern the political and economic make-up of the former Yugoslavia, and I have also done research into the mechanisms of self-management so that my topic always was the analysis of social development in the region of former Yugoslavia from the breakdown of Austro-Hungary until the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we place this in a time context, then this would be the period from 1918 until the present time, of course with some indications of earlier times?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Of course, with an introduction that also partly also encompasses the political development of Serbia. Following the Serb revolutions in 1804 and 1815, and also the political life of Croatia as part of the Habsburg monarchy, this would be an introductory part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, your research and your scientific interests range from events in the region of former Yugoslavia, the creation of a common state, and then, finally, the disintegration of that state?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the topic that you will talk to us about is the process of disintegration of former Yugoslavia as a process of disintegration which, in fact, had, as a consequence, the events, a part of which, maybe the most horrible part, is the event from Bosnia that this case also deals with, so I would like to ask you to give us a sort of framework, a brief introduction, in a spontaneous talk, and then I will ask questions as I feel necessary. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the subject matter of Yugoslavia is one of the most difficult in Europe in the 20th century, primarily for the following reason: I could say that the contradictions of the world met in a very confined area on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say, within a community that was multi-national, multi-religious, even multi-civilisational, if you wish. May I recall on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, over a span of 80 years, there were five wars, and each and every one of these wars broke out among the different peoples of Yugoslavia and ended up in genocide, in ethnic cleansing. I have to present certain facts here that are relevant to the understanding of this subject matter, although it is a very difficult one. You know very well that the creation of states, its break-up, and then wars, liberation wars, wars of conquest, et cetera, begin by being preceded by the establishment of a certain ideology and the establishment of certain political programs. Therefore, in order to understand what happened, we must say a few words precisely about these political ideologies and political programs that came into being before Yugoslavia was created. The political ideology either of the Serbs or of the Croats or the Macedonians or the Slovenes, et cetera, has a certain aspect of its own, one that is aimed at creating a state of its own, as I usually put it; namely, every nation, even if it is a micro-nation consisting of several hundreds of thousands of inhabitants or very big nations --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you, Professor, but could you please speak slower because of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: The Serb state idea and the Croat state idea came into being exactly in the mid 19th century. I wish to point out that this was before Bismarck united Germany or Garibaldi united Italy. I do not wish to say that the Croats and the Serbs were at a higher level development because of that. On the contrary, I simply wish to say that that is when they came into being. Allow me to point out what was the substance of the Serb state idea and what was the substance of the Croatian state idea and may I point out the extent to which they corresponded to one another and, on the other hand, the extent to which they were opposed to one another? There are many sources that I cannot quote here that concern the Serb state idea. I shall refer to but two that are of capital importance. I shall not refer to the statesman Garasanin, I am just going to mention the person who wanted to create a Greater Serbia within Dusan's empire. Namely, the history of Europe shows that nations primarily wish to have a state which covers something that did exist in the past. That would be the first principle. And within that state, they wish to include even the most distant branches of their ethnos, even the most distant ones. These were the ideas of a greater Germany, greater Bulgaria, greater Serbia, greater Croatia, et cetera. The ideology of the great Serb linguistic reformer who had world wide recognition, Vuk Stefanovic Karadzic was his name, it relies upon the German theory of the nation, and the German theory of the nation says one language, one nation. Safarik established this in 1826 and then Vuk Karadzic in 1849 elaborated on this idea, and proceeding from the true fact that Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Montenegrins, et cetera -- excluding Slovenia -- speak one language, which is true. He deduced on that basis that this is one nation because it is one language. So all the people who speak Serbian, i.e. Croatian, and he omits that, are Serbs. If one looks at how widespread the Serb language is, then one comes to the conclusion that Serbs spanned the area from Trieste to Saloniki and Istanbul. In 1873 a map was issued on how widespread the Serbs were, and you will see what this looks like on this map. May I show it now here on the ELMO? Is that all right? Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt my learned friend? Your Honours, I must point out that there is no English translation of what appears in this map. My learned friend, I believe, will submit an English translation of the writing that appears on this map before the Defence case is concluded or at least before we cross-examine the witness in the course of this week, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an historical map and the inscription uses the Cyrillic alphabet that is used in Serbia. The Defence can provide for a translation of this but only in terms of the Latin alphabet, the Latin inscription, but these are geographical names so we cannot really translate them. What the Defence can do during the presentation of its case is have translated the description of this map. However, Professor Bilandzic is going to read this out now, so that will become part of the transcript, but we are going to try to provide a translation during the course of the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it's sufficient for you to have this explanation, that Professor Bilandzic is going to give? You will get an inscription of what is on the map, that is to say, the geographical names because geographical names cannot really be translated. What do you think of that, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. As Your Honours say, the source of map and those details, since they have not been translated, it is not possible for the Prosecution to get to the source of the document, to ascertain from where the document has been obtained, and if my learned friend, through the witness, would give sufficient details in order to identify, in order to enable us to identify the source of the document, certainly the Prosecution would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I think that Mr. Mikulicic has already said that, so there is going to be a translation either into the English or into the French language, and that will suffice. I think that we can continue with the evidence of Professor Bilandzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Another document whose author is Jovan Cvijic, president of the Serbian Academy of Sciences, a professor at the Sorbonne in Paris --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Professor. Could you please be so kind as to explain the document that is in front of you on the ELMO for the Trial Chamber and then we're going to move on to the other document, and please, whenever you use a document, would you mention the source, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: All right. This document was published by Serbia in 1873 on the basis of an analysis of how widespread the Serb language is and, as you can see on the extreme left, in the corner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Professor, excuse me for interrupting you. Perhaps this is not very pleasant for you, but could you explain the map to us in the following way, by turning to the ELMO, because if you show it only on your screen, we cannot see it. However, if you show this on the ELMO, then we will be able to see it too, if this is not too uncomfortable for you. I'm sorry, Mr. Mikulicic, for having interrupted.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: You see, this line here is the peninsula of Istria, just before Trieste, and then there is a line going to Zagreb almost, and then it continues toward Hungary and it goes toward the Hungarian border. It includes Vojvodina. Then it moves toward the Danube, near the Bulgarian Serbian border, approximately. It includes the border zone with Bulgaria and it goes down to Macedonia, but below this green colour it says Serbo Macedonians, because they are also considered to be Serbs and they spread all the way to Saloniki. So this entire thesis is based on the fact of how widespread the Serb language is, so I repeat, this thesis is one language, one nation; one nation, one state. So that is the heart of the matter. And now may I just mention in a few words the world renowned authority of the Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts, Jovan Cvijic, who is President of the Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts who presented the following thesis that the same thing that we are showing here, he said literally from Trieste to Saloniki and to Istanbul, all of that is an uncrystallised ethnic mass which has not yet created firm state and political structures. This mass consists of 9.625.200 and all -- and this entire mass, so to speak, speaks Serbian, and at that point in time, and that is 1908 when the kingdom of the Serbs was recognised and it was recognised way back, the Berlin congress in 1878, in that Serbia, as a state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I am having difficulty hearing the English translation. Would the technical engineer please attend to this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Serbia, which was then called the kingdom of Serbia, had 2.700.000, a population of 2.700.000 and the territory that speaks Serbian has 9.625.200 citizens. In this analysis made by Jovan Cvijic, President of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, which was entitled "The Annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb issue," it says that Bosnia and Herzegovina is a central Serb country and, he adds, this is not similar to Alsace Lorraine, between France and Germany, but it is similar to the importance that the area of Moscow has for Russia. If you look at the map, you will see that Bosnia and Herzegovina is to the west of Serbia and that Croatia continues. So Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor. Could you please -- when you're saying something to us, you will have to forget what you have in front of you on the table. Please think only of that which you have at the ELMO so that we can all follow what you are saying. We are just getting used to all these technical facilities too, and we know it's difficult for you, but, please, just point to the things that are on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: You see, on this ELMO ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Professor, also, all the documents that you wish to show to us have to be registered, they have to get a certain number.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D15.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: So if you would look on the map, Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot be the central part of -- a central Serbian country because it's situated between Croatia and Serbia. However, the Serbian Academy has the right to claim this because it sets out from the fact that Croatians speak Serbian and belong to the Serbs. Also, only they're of the Catholic faith. In that sense, Bosnia is a central Serbian country. I would like to finish with this on the Serbian idea of -- national idea. Now I will talk about the Croatian national idea. Croatia had a different historical development. In brief, it was a kingdom until 1925. Then it entered into a personal union with Bulgaria so that both states, Hungary and Croatia, had one king, who was Crowned both as the Hungarian and the Croatian king. This was in 1102. In 1526, because the Turks had started to conquer that area because Hungary became very weak so that Croatia and Hungary accepted the Austrian empire, the Habsburg Monarch as their king, since then, until 1918, until the creation of Yugoslavia, the Austrian empire, each Austrian emperor from Maria-Theresia and so on, would also be crowned as the King of Croatia. So Croatia had three elements of state hood. It had a name, the kingdom of Croatia, it always had an established territory, it had its assembly, some kind of parliament, it had a Viceroy who was called Ban. In a parliamentary debate in Hungary, the Croatian Ban, on the occasion of an attempt to apply Hungarian laws in Croatia, stated the famous sentence: (statement in Latin), in other words one kingdom has no right in this case, the Hungarian, to impose its laws on another kingdom, i.e., Croatia. Why did I mention this? This position that Croatia within the Habsburg monarchy and that it had such a status is the foundation of the state idea of Croatia. Croats comprised 5.6 of the population of the whole Habsburg monarchy, and their idea, their programme, political programme, which was formulated by the Viceroy, i.e. Ban Jelacic, and a national movement that Croatia would be forever within the Habsburg monarchy, but to have this monarchy federalised in such a way that Croatia unifies all the countries of the Austro-Hungarian, these would be all the southern Slavs, and you see this is Slovenia, this is Croatia, Vojvodina, Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that all of these countries gather around Croatia and get -- receive the status of the third member of the Habsburg monarchy. Because as far as -- as you know, Austria and Hungary had a dominant position within the Habsburg empire. And here, they wanted to create a third unit. Another thing that's very important. This is the so-called dualism of the Habsburg monarchy. If the Austrian empire and the Habsburg monarchy accepted the Croatian solution, then Austria would be tri -- it would have three parts and not two parts, it wouldn't be a dual. This was the main concept of the Croatian state idea. I would also like to mention two more concepts, one is the Yugoslav concept. In Croatia, a strong Yugoslav movement developed in Croatia in the second half of the 19th century. Whose elite imagined the creation of a greater Yugoslav state, but as a federation with the intimate desire that Croatia would be in a hegemonic position. Symbolically, in 1866 there was an academy of arts and sciences formed in Zagreb but it wasn't named as the Croatian academy, it was called the Yugoslav South Slav Academy because this was supposed to be an academy of Croats, Serbs, Slovenes and Bulgarians, if you please. So this is a marginal political idea, mostly entertained by the intelligentsia. The third idea that had no chance at all was the formation of an independent state, so these were the concepts. So the Serb state idea which goes for the expansion of Serbia, the Croatian state idea which goes for the creation of a third member of the Habsburg empire, the so-called southern Slav unit in the confederation with Hungary and Austria. And there is also the Croatian idea to join Serbs to Montenegro, but this would then have to be a federation, so I move to the next question: What happened in brief in World War I? Unfortunately, the countries of southern Slavs from Austria; Croats, Serbs, and Slovenes. The citizens of Vojvodina, Bosnia, Croatia, Slovenia, were unfortunately in the war against Serbia during the entire four years, they were actually the occupiers there. The Croatian assembly, as well as the parliamentarians in the Austrian parliament, in World War I, almost until the disintegration of Austro-Hungary, took the position of the trialism that I mentioned earlier, i.e. the southern Slavs within the Habsburg monarchy would have their own state, recognising the Austrian emperor. Serbia had a different idea. In 1915, it received agreement of the Russian empire, Great Britain, France, Italy, as the powers of Allies to expand in such a way that a part of the Slavic countries from the Austrian -- Austro-Hungarian empire would be joined to Serbia. This is the so-called concept of Greater Serbia. Just roughly these -- this is the secret London contract agreement which was signed between Serbia and the allies in 1915.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D16.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: As you can see on the map, after the central -- the fall of the central powers of Austro-Hungary, Serbia is given the territory which goes along this blue line. Excuse me. It takes the area close to Virovitica, but it is this red line and it goes all the way to the sea, so that Serbia would get Bosnia and Herzegovina, a good part of Dalmatia and also the eastern part of Croatia. However, things did not quite develop in that way because Serbia lost the support of Russia in 1917, and Wilson, United States President, did not agree so easily to the contributions and the secret agreements that the peoples -- whereby peoples would be joined to one or the other side, so that this could not be carried out exactly in this way. Something else was carried out. As I said, the Croatian citizens who were in the war against Austro-Hungary -- for Austro-Hungary, they were pretty faithful to Austro-Hungary and generally the southern Slavs accept the Serbs who, of course, felt in the fight against Serbia felt quite uncomfortable and escaped from the army, would cross the front lines and go as volunteers, even a few Croats. But on the whole, the Croatian assembly parliament, until the end of the Austro-Hungarian empire, mainly remained on the positions of the mentioned trialism, i.e., the state within the Austro-Hungarian empire. When Austria was in agony, then the parliamentarians in Vienna, Slovenes and Croats as well as the empire Croatian assembly, decided to create one state. Outside of Austro-Hungary, if it should fall apart, meaning to create a state which would comprise -- now I will show this on the map so would you please show this to the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honour, the map that Professor Bilandzic took is a new map which we didn't have time to prepare because Professor Bilandzic in the course of his work prepared it today, so for the needs of the evidence, we will photocopy that later, but for now Professor Bilandzic will tell us what it is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as long as I have a copy of the translation prior to the cross-examination in order for the Prosecution to do that effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Would you please continue?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D17.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I will draw a line which will divide Serbia and the countries of Austro-Hungary, the Slav Austro-Hungarian countries, and the line goes like this: West of this line, there are Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Slovenia, and Vojvodina. At the time of Austro-Hungary's agony, these countries form a state. At the end of October 1917, they name it the state of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs. At that time, Serbia has the idea, since Austro-Hungary is in agony, to simply join these countries to Serbia, meaning to avoid the creation of a different southern Slav state because besides Serbia and Montenegro, there would be another state, and this should be avoided. It wants to expand Serbia with new countries and it would have the order of a centralist kingdom, according to the political system model that was in Serbia from 1903 to 1918. So two completely opposing ideas clashed like that, and this state, the capital of which was Zagreb, entered into negotiations with Serbia and on November 9th, 1918, an agreement was reached about the creation of new Yugoslavia, so this new state would enter Zagreb with Belgrade, but it was demanded for this to be a confederation, the state itself, whose capital was now Zagreb, which Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina entered, was organised within itself as a federation, so you would have governments in Ljubjana, Zagreb, Sarajevo, Split, and Novi Sad. So this federation would enter into confederative relations with the kingdom of Serbia which was already before that joined by Montenegro. The president of the Serbian government signed such an agreement for the creation of Yugoslavia on this basis. But the Serbian government, having studied the Geneva declaration -- I don't know if I stated already that this happened in Geneva, so the Geneva declaration -- the Serbian government refused this thesis with two arguments: First, we are one nation, one people, Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, they are one nation. So one nation cannot enter into state contracts amongst itself, within itself. Secondly, what you are proposing from Zagreb is a copy of the Austro-Hungarian dualism, meaning to say, the dual monarchy, so that then we would have both a Serb monarchy, i.e. a Yugoslav monarchy, so this was rejected. Yugoslavia was created as a centralist state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic and Professor Bilandzic, after these two arguments that we have listened to now, I think it is time for a break of 20 minutes, and then I would like to ask you to continue with your testimony. So now we adjourn for a 20-minute break. --- Recess at 4.00 p.m. --- Resumed at 4.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic and Professor Bilandzic, we can continue. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor Bilandzic, after the break, we can continue with your testimony. You mentioned that the first Yugoslavia in 1918 was organised as an expanded Serbia. Would you please explain this for us, what is the background of this claim of yours, but please turn your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Two or three sentences before I respond to that question. Why was a state created in the agony of Austro-Hungary in 1917 which was joined by Slovenia, Bosnia, Vojvodina and Croatia, and why did it agree to become abolished and to become part of Serbia? This is a complex situation. And it's about the fact that Serbs -- Serb, Italian, and French troops, as the troops of entente, freely entered because this was the territory of the defeated Habsburg monarchy, that's one thing. Second, the Croatian peasant population, after the example of the Russian revolution, started to create chaos, rebellion, robberies, looting of rich homes, and the Croatian political ruling class agreed to enter -- for the Serb troops to enter in order to stifle these rebellions. The new state didn't have an army or the police because it was created in the agony of Austro-Hungary so that it accepted this concept of the creation of such a Yugoslavia, i.e., a centralist one. And in response to your question, this is about the fact that the government of the kingdom of Serbia, working precisely in the spirit of the concept of creating one state, abolished the structures in all the other countries, meaning the governments in Zagreb, the government in Sarajevo, the government in Novi Sad, and the government in Ljubjana and all of their parliaments, and instead of those historic countries, the whole new state was divided into 33 administrative regions, subject to the Royal rule in Belgrade, so they disappeared from political life, the historical countries which lasted for thousands of years, so to say, and also their state structures disappeared. And this is how a centralist state was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, in such a situation, do you see elements of conflict which would later be demonstrated in events in this region?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: As soon as the centralist Yugoslavia was established, even a few days before it was established, in Croatia -- I should not say overnight but within a few months' time, a massive national movement was created and Stjepan Radic came to its head, the leader of the Croatian peasants' party, because peasants were 80 percent of the population, he practically came the charismatic national leader, and Croatian parliamentarians rejected the recognition of this newly established state and this went on for several years. After that, they did enter the parliament of the kingdom of Yugoslavia after all, where great polemics continued because the political parties of some other countries, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course not all of them but some of them, embraced the positions of federalism, namely, Radic's Croats said that things had to go back to 1918, that is to say, not to recognise the establishment of that state, and they tried, through the parliament, to renew the federation instead of a centralist state. Terrible quarrels broke out in the parliament, and on the 28th of June, 1928, a member of parliament, Punisa Racic, took out his pistol, and during a heated quarrelsome debate in parliament, he killed three leaders of the Croats, and two were seriously injured. That was the leadership of the -- the political leadership of Croatia that was in the federal parliament, they were killed literally in their parliamentary seats. After that, the Croats refused to take part in political parliamentary life, and then King Alexander came to face a dilemma. What should he do? The danger of a revolution was looming over him. He invited the successor of Stjepan Radic, this was Dr. Vlatko Macek, and offered him the amputation of Slovenia and Croatia. According to this amputation, Croatia would have received 54.2 percent of the territory of the kingdom of Croatia that existed within Austro-Hungary. In the negotiations between the King and the Croats, he was -- actually, a man named Svetozar Pribicevic who was leader of the Serbs in Croatia, conducted these negotiations on behalf of the King, and the Croats could not agree to this because only 54.2 percent of their territories would remain in their hands, and so they rejected this. And there's another reason for this rejection: The entente sought a stable Yugoslavia, and they needed a stable Yugoslavia for two reasons: First of all, Yugoslavia was supposed to be an impediment to the possible renewal of German Imperialism, and secondly, Yugoslavia should be a state within the small entente, that was supposed to be a sanitary cordon against Bolshevik Russia, that is to say the Baltic states, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Yugoslavia so this was the "cordon sanitaire." So the great powers supported Yugoslavia, and this amputation never occurred, but then a practical question was raised: Could parliamentarianism be continued after the assassination of the leadership of Croatian politics. This could not continue in this way not only because of them but also because of Serbia. In the kingdom of Yugoslavia, Serbs accounted for 36 percent of the population so if, for example, the British model of democracy were to be applied and if truly fair and free and honourable parliament elections were to take place, Serbs would always be a minority in that parliament, and the regime of the kingdom of Yugoslavia could not be perpetuated because the non-Serb nations were a majority. So the King decided in favour of a military dictatorship, and he appointed a general of his as Prime Minister, and they went even a step further. It is not only that a Croatian -- the names of Croatia and Macedonia and others were abolished but also the name of Serbia itself was abolished. It was hoped that this could turn into a melting pot and that a Yugoslav nation could be created and therefore that statistics should be abolished. I'm sorry. I can't remember the name. Please help me with this. Oh, yes, a census, a census. The census never said Serb, Croat, Slovene, et cetera, we were all Yugoslavs, you know, there were no separate nations of this kind. Of course, this was utopia, this was a delusion, and this went on until 1934. In 1934, the Ustashe organisation, this was a pro-fascist organisation from Croatia, and they were assisted by Bulgarian and Macedonian revolutionaries, and they killed King Alexander in Marseilles, and a year later parliamentarianism was established once again but there were different manipulations involved and I will not elaborate on that further. It is important to say the following: The Yugoslav society split according to three different lines: First, there was a bloc of centralists, unitarianists, and there was a federal bloc too, and within the federal bloc, within every national group there were also fractions in favour of breaking up Yugoslavia, but then this is also a broad subject that I cannot get into now. It is only under the pressure that was brought to bear by Great Britain and France that an agreement was finally reached between Belgrade and Zagreb. Belgrade gave Zagreb an autonomous state unit which was called the Banovina of Croatia, so this historic name of Croatia was reinstated, and it came into being in the following manner: Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided, Croatia got 66.000 square kilometres which is about nine and a half thousand square kilometres more than the territory of the following socialist republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mean Croatia after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you, Professor, but you mentioned just now Bosnia-Herzegovina as describing these events. If we are to go back a bit, we will see that in this area, the primary tension, so to speak, was between Serbia and Croatia. Where did Bosnia stand in this context?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Oh, very well. Now I wanted to speak about Bosnia in greater detail anyway, but perhaps by way of an introduction, I could say a few things. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, I don't have the accurate figures here, but I won't make any major mistakes. During the Austro-Hungarian rule, 43 percent of the population of Bosnia were Serbs 32 percent were Muslims, and 23 percent were Croats. The Croatian political idea counted on the possibility of annexing Bosnia according to that idea of trialism that we've been referring to. According to the Berlin agreement, Bosnia-Herzegovina came under the rule of Vienna and Budapest and in 1908 it was annexed, Austro-Hungary tried to create a Bosniak nation because they thought that the power of a state can create nations. Sometimes this is possible, but sometimes it is not. When is it not possible? When the process of the creation of states has gone so far that they no longer agree to a melting pot. Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not accept the concept of a Bosniak nation, so Serbs and Croats remained only, and this concept failed. Croat politicians in 1908, during the annexation sent a message to Belgrade -- I'm quoting from memory -- if Bosnia is not annexed but is handed over to the kingdom of Serbia, we would welcome this. That is what Croats say. Croats from Zagreb say that. However, if we live to see such a fate that the great powers do not give you Bosnia, you should be happy if it falls into the hands of Austro-Hungary because we are going to work on uniting all these countries into one state according to this idea of trialism. So how should I put this? Zagreb and Belgrade -- we've elaborated on that considerably so I'm just repeating it now -- had aspirations to take over all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially their extremists on both sides. Only a compromise could ensure a solution, just or unjust. In 1939, the Serbs and the Croats, seven days before the outbreak of the Second World War, they divided up Bosnia. Approximately, because I don't have the exact figures now, the greater part of the territory came under the rule not of Serbia but of Yugoslavia -- I'm sorry, I just have to give this brief explanation. If the Banovina of Croatia was established and it took about one third of the territory of Bosnia and it was created, it was recognised it is an autonomous land, the King, or rather, the Prince, the Regency, they accepted this. And if you look at the map, what has actually happened? The entire remaining part of Yugoslavia, that is to say a larger part of Bosnia, Vojvodina, Montenegro, Macedonia remained as a single entity, and the ruling class, the Serb ruling class, wanted to create from this remainder of Yugoslavia the so-called Serb autonomous unit, so even before the Second World War it would have had three units: Slovenia, under the name of Dravska Banovina, Croatia under the name of Banovina Croatia, and the so-called Serb lands, the remainder. And that is approximately about two thirds of Yugoslavia, perhaps even more than that. I personally think -- although in historiography there is no proof to this, that already in 1939 there was an attempt to split up Yugoslavia into three parts: Slovenia, Croatia, and the Serb lands. So this was only a question of days. However, after seven days, seven days after this agreement came into being, the Second World War broke out, and that is what I wish to say about the kingdom of Yugoslavia, and now with your permission, I should like to move onto the war between 1941 and 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, perhaps before you move on to this other part, perhaps we should go back a bit? You explained to us what were the forces of history that were in play and what kind of interests clashed in the area. Please tell us, tell the Chamber, what was the structure of the population in this area in terms of religion, in terms of civilisational development, industrial development, do you see any forces of conflict in play there that would perhaps, in the near future, lead to the events that actually ensued?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: It's a known fact that Yugoslavia was multi-national. It's also well-known that Yugoslavia did not recognise the existence of nations, nationalities, but it contained within itself five nations: The Serb nation, Croatian, Slovene, Macedonian, which was not only not recognised but you couldn't even say Macedonian or Macedonia, and also it's very debatable about Montenegro. A part of Montenegrins consider themselves to be Montenegrins and the rest consider themselves Serbs. Secondly, Yugoslavia was a multi-confessional country. Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro are countries of the Orthodox faith, 45.5 percent, Croatia and Slovenia are Catholic countries, 30.8 percent, and Muslim, Sunni, 17 percent. But it's even more important that the degree of development, the differences among the Yugoslav countries, were seven to one, which means that the least developed parts of Yugoslavia would, if we mark them as one, the rate of -- the rate of development would be 700 percent of greater difference. So we also want -- 1500 years from the arrival to the Balkans and to this area, these peoples were never in one state. The first time this happened was in 1918, so that they carry with them a stamp, a cultural civilisational stamp, the western part of Croatia, Slovenia, Vojvodina, which is Serb, have that Danubian central European stamp which was left by Austro-Hungary which was a pretty solid state at a high level of civilisation, which is a country with a rule of law regardless of the fact that it was accused as the prisoner of nations. The eastern part was under the Byzantine influence, for five hundred years it was under Turkish occupation, so there are civilisational differences here. So that the creation of a common state from such varied elements could not be expected to be a successful process of organic capillary linking among the peoples into a stable political and social community. This just simply did not happen. If you permit me now about the war? As you know, war is always a test of the situation. War frees, releases the most savage as well as the most noble -- how shall I say? -- moments in human society. So the war of 1941 to 1945, unfortunately -- I was a Communist for 50 years, a member of the Central Committee. However, unfortunately we have to change the historiography that we Communists imposed on the public. It did not happen the way we told generations from elementary schools, the way we presented it through mass media textbooks. It didn't quite happen that way. In 1941, Yugoslavia, on April 6th, it was attacked, which is also one more argument saying that it could not determine its own path. We said that it was created to a large part by the entente powers, Great Britain, France, Italy, and we have a negative example. This is a relatively small country which was an instrument in the hands of the German Reich. Hitler offered Yugoslavia to sign the Tripartite Agreement, but it didn't agree to that. In 1941, the Yugoslav army gave absolutely no resistance to the Wehrmacht. The Wehrmacht, Bulgarian and Hungarian armies entered Yugoslavia without a struggle, weapons were laid down without a struggle. Germany created Greater Croatia, Hitler created Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: He joined Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina into one state and named it the Independent Republic of Croatia, the Independent State of Croatia. This was a quisling creation, a puppet state under the protection of Hitler and Mussolini, and the state, the Ustashe state, accepted to implement Nazi-fascist racial laws. It took out its sword against the Serbs, Jews, Gypsies, Romanies with the aim of creating from that state, an as-ethnically-homogeneous-as-possible Croatia, treating Muslims in Bosnia as -- and this is the term used by the Ustashas -- as the flower of Croatian people who converted to Islam but they were still Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Regarding the Muslim nations, could you please explain how a Muslim nationality nation came about in this region?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: This is a subject that requires a lot of research. In brief, Catholicism, which spread from the Vatican, and to Christianising the Balkan area, including Croatia, sometime in the Middle Ages required quite strongly that rituals in churches could not be conducted in the national language. This caused a lot of resistance in Bosnia and Herzegovina so a part of those people accepted that well-known religion which developed in other parts of Europe as well, the Patarines (phonetics) -- I think there is another name for it; it doesn't matter right now -- and then when the Turks conquered Bosnia and Herzegovina, that part, as well as other parts of the people, accepted Islam and Muslims. Absolutely there is no doubt about that. They are Slavs, just like Serbs, Croats and the others are, they are Slavs, but they just converted to Islam. When the independent state of Croatia as a puppet state was created, they quite voluntarily accepted -- a part of them accepted the Banovina Hrvatska, I mean the puppet state, the independent state of Croatia; and during the kingdom of Yugoslavia, because they were, just like the Croats, persecuted, they were a faction, one faction of them. But this was not a decisive factor. Communists later will decide to recognise them as a nation, and this will be 1969. And for the first time in 1971, the census includes them as a nation, and this is something that was started by the Communist party of Yugoslavia. So when the independent state of Croatia was created and when it started to introduce the Nazi-fascist order, of course, this could not remain without the resistance of the Serbs and also democratically-oriented Croats. Serbia turned into a zone of occupation and it was reduced to the territory it had before the Balkan wars, before the expansion of Serbia. Kosovo was joined to Vojvodina -- I mean Albania, Macedonia to Bulgaria, Vojvodina, Dravska Banovina to Hungary and so forth. This is really not important at this time. Something else is important. There is the question of what will happen with us, who with us, with Croats, Serbs, Slovenes and the others, when the Second World War is over. A part of the people believed in the thousand-year-old new Ordnung, Hitler's famous new order that will last for a thousand years. But, of course, the majority of the people, deep inside themselves, were convinced that Germany will lose the war, and this was something that they wanted to prepare for. I'm speaking now, first of all, about the elites. The government of the kingdom of Serbia escaped to London. From London, they organised, i.e., better to say it established, determined the policy for its followers during the war. The policy was as follows: The democratic wing of the Croatian people, represented by the pro-British Croatian Peasants Party, Radic that I mentioned who was killed, his party was pro-British, pro-Allies. The Royal government, they believed the following: Be quiet. Do not go into war against the occupiers. Wait until the end of World War II. The allies will come, they will liberate us, and then we will resolve all our questions. So there is no fighting. The Communist party of Yugoslavia right away in 1941, on the 4th of July, twelve days after the Wehrmacht attacked Russia, started a rebellion, rose against the occupiers, and started a war, a cruel war. This war was conducted by Tito, and with all the downfalls, all the successes and the failures, in 1943, in late 1943, Tito had an army of 300.000 people. This is a respectable army. The Royal government in London reacted very strongly towards the partisan movement and towards Tito's army, ordering its military Minister, Draza Mihailovic, he was the leader of the Chetniks and who, in the middle of the war, had about 100.000 people, that he must destroy Tito's army at any cost. Of course, against Tito's army, the NDH, the puppet state and also Nedic's army fought against that army as well, so that all of the different political forces fought. Why did the Royal government ask the Chetniks to destroy the partisan forces? Because the Communist party of Yugoslavia had a programme of liquidation of Greater Serbia and Greater Croatia, which means liquidation of that Serbia which ruled Yugoslavia but also the NDH even more because it was a puppet state. So the Communists reject the concept of Serb bourgeoisie, Croat bourgeoisie, Yugoslav bourgeoisie and the forces of the bourgeoisie in general and they offered a compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was the gist of the compromise from the Communist party of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: It stated the Croats will get a state in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of a state?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: It will be a state but within the Yugoslav federation. The same thing will be for the Slovenes, for the Macedonians, for the Montenegrins, and for Bosnia-Herzegovina. "You Serbs must return to Serbia and you will be a republic just like the other republics." As opposed to that, the Royal government had also a project of what will happen at the end of World War II. According to that project -- there are documents, there are maps here, but I don't really want to present them -- but this is the Yugoslav People's Army and the old regime published these documents, and these are well-known to the whole of Yugoslavia. There would be a much stronger regime established after World War II because Croatia would be left with only 20 percent of its territory, there would be only Zagreb and a few other municipalities, regions in north-western Croatia would remain so, but the border between Greater Serbia would be set on the river Kupa together with Slovenia. So this was the most disgusting, the most extreme form of the renewal of Greater Serb Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who propagated such a form of the renewal of Greater Serb Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: There is a document, an assistant of Draza Mihailovic, his name is Stevan Moljevic, he's a member of the Central Committee of the Chetnik movement. I, of course, have to skip a lot of things. Draza Mihailovic, General, who at the end of 1941 became a Minister of the kingdom of Yugoslavia, so he was a contact with the Royal government in London from which he received directives, he was the leader of the Chetnik movement. He was that in 1941, 1942, and 1943, and in the Western media, he was declared as the Robin Hood of the Balkan mountains, as the greatest guerrilla in Europe. Some forces today are preparing in Washington an agreement as the first and greatest guerrilla fighter in Europe, and really, he did create an army of 100.000 Chetniks. But that army waged war only against the partisans, and this was ethnically a purely Serb army without any other members and it was a terror for non-Serbian people. There is a terrible paradox in this. Churchill told King Peter in 1944, in January, "Please sack Draza Mihailovic, dismiss him. Pull out of an impossible situation. You are having contacts with Germans, Italians, and the Independent State of Croatia, and you are not fighting against the Germans. So we have a situation here where you are an allied country, Yugoslavia, but your army in Yugoslavia, the Chetniks, are cooperating with our enemies, with the Germans." When Eden asked him -- and to go on. So Churchill, Stalin, and Roosevelt, on December 1st, 1943, in Teheran, reached the decision to reject Draza Mihailovic and to accept Tito as the only leader of the national uprising in Yugoslavia, the popular uprising in Yugoslavia, and to provide arms to him. To Eden's question on one occasion, "Why are you helping Communists and not the Chetniks?" he said "I am helping those who are killing more Germans." I think this is just an aside, but it's not that important. So the main clash in the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1941, 1942 is the clash between the partisan army and the Communist party of Yugoslavia, of course, which was asking for six federal units and the army of the kingdom of Yugoslavia which wants to renew the Greater Serbian Yugoslavia in a much more drastic form than it was between the two World Wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me just for a second. I would like to clarify some facts. You stated that the army of Draza Mihailovic was actually an ethnically composed army comprising only one people, those were Serbs. On the other hand, the partisan army, how was that conceived from that standpoint?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: It is a very interesting and important issue, you know, but it kept changing. In 1941, from July until November, Serbia was the bastion of the partisan movement with a total of 25.000 partisans. Also Montenegro, which then had about 30.000 partisans, so Tito had 50.000 partisans, approximately, in the first two months of the uprising from Serbia and Montenegro. However, at the end of November 1941, this army of Tito's was broken up. Out of a total of about 60.000 partisans in Serbia and Montenegro, only 6.000 remained and they had to flee to Bosnia. So in Serbia, from the beginning of 1941 until the Red Army came in 1944, practically -- we used to call this "revolution" in Communist terminology, a socialist revolution -- the socialist revolution was then quelled. Tito then left Serbia and Montenegro and went to Bosnia and Croatia. In Bosnia and Croatia, he created this army of 300.000 people in Bosnia, Croatia, and Slovenia, of course. I am going to give you some interesting figures now. This army of 300.000 people consisted of 96 brigades, there were divisions, cores, et cetera, and out of this total, 38 brigades or 40 percent were in Croatia, in Bosnia 23, in Slovenia 17, in Montenegro 6, in Serbia 5, and in Vojvodina 5. There is just one more thing I have to add to this. Bearing in mind the future state structure of Yugoslavia, Tito and the Communist party, from 1941 to 1945, had a military structure according to the future republics. That is to say that every republic had headquarters, a general staff of its own partisans, though there was a general staff of Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina respectively. He, Tito, coordinated things with his own small general staff and also a small group of divisions, three to five, but the remaining 37 divisions are under the command of republican headquarters. So, of course, in addition to this military structure, a political structure was created too; also the national assemblies of these future republics and also provisional governments. So already from 1941 there was a federal structure, which meant death to a Greater Serb Yugoslavia and to the quisling Greater Croatia, namely the independent state of Croatia. So this was the main clash between those who were aspiring for power after the Second World War, namely, the Royal government in London and the Communist party on the other hand. In 1944, because Tito did not have Serbia then, he asked Stalin to help him in liberating Serbia. Stalin ordered Marshall Tolbuhin, the commander of the Third Ukrainian Front, to make available to Tito the strongest forces possible. Marshall Tolbuhin gave the 57th Soviet army to Tito, the 14th mechanised corps of General Zhdanov, four divisions -- I can't remember the name now -- the storm forces, and Dimitrov, the well-known leader of the Comintern, on the 9th of September, 1944, he took over Bulgaria and he also sent his forces to Serbia, and Tito on the other hand, from Western Yugoslavia, that is to say, from Bosnia and Croatia, he sent nine partisan divisions to Serbia. In Serbia itself in 1944, he established five divisions from the Serb people who lived there, and in the autumn of 1944, the Communist party managed to get Serbia. So the Royal government and Draza Mihailovic ended the war at that point. So that was where the main clash was within Yugoslavia between two completely, absolutely opposite irreconcilable ideas, state ideas too. However, the rift among the people themselves was even greater within each nation -- this was a conflict between nations in part. But, for example, in Croatia, when the Ustashe persecuted the Serbs, Serbia, of course, which was tied up by the Wehrmacht, could not help the Serbs in Croatia, but the Serbs in Bosnia strongly resisted the independent state of Croatia in 1941. So there was a conflict between the Serbs and Croats in Croatia and in Bosnia -- I mean, there were some Croats who were supporting the Ustashes and then there was yet another war. That is a civil war within each and every nation. Croat Communists were fighting against Croat Ustashes, Serb Chetniks were fighting against Serb partisans, and Slovene partisans were fighting against Slovenes who were in the democrat forces. So this is a triple war within the nations, between the nations, and then these global forces, Tito's army, et cetera, et cetera. So that is how the Second World War came to an end in which the Communists won and created a federation consisting of six states, six republics. I say republic states because the constitutions treat them as states, the constitution from 1946, the constitution from 1963, the constitution from 1971, and in particular, the constitution of 1974. And now a few words about Tito's Yugoslavia. The Communists thought that they had resolved all the issues relevant in Yugoslavia. That isn't the very nature of ideology. "Before us there was only darkness, and when we come to power, then comes welfare, well-being, a new civilisation, happiness," et cetera, et cetera. So this was a wonderful utopia which became an opium for over a billion inhabitants of our planet. Communism embraced Yugoslavia too, especially the younger generation. The Communists said that they found an ideal solution to the national issue and, indeed so, they did find an ideal solution from the point of view of creating states. But they proceeded from a Communist thesis that nations are a product of capitalism, and as soon as the capitalist order is toppled, as soon as the bourgeoisie is no longer in power, as soon as the working class comes to power, then the process of the withering away of nations will begin. So we don't have to pay any attention to whether these are republics or not. The political system, the economic system, cultural policy, economic policy, foreign policy, military policy, do not have to deal with the federation. They don't have to be imbued with federalism. On the contrary, there is no Communism without centralism. So everything should be centralised in Belgrade. Therefore, what Croatia's policy will be like in the fields of culture, education, economic affairs, et cetera, will not be established by you in Zagreb but by the politburo of the Communist party of Yugoslavia in Belgrade. What Serb policy will be like will not be determined by Serbs, by the Republic of Serbia, but it will be sustained by us. Who are we? The leadership of Yugoslavia. The politburo and the government. This is valid in the case of Slovenia also and everyone else. Therefore, the Communists did practically introduce a federation, but all of government in all fields, foreign policy, military policy, interior policy, legal policy, cultural policy, educational policy, everything was centralised in the leadership of the Communist party of Yugoslavia and the federal government. At the beginning, things worked well. There was no resistance to this. Why? Because nationalist forces, chauvinist forces of Serbia, Croatia, and the others, were defeated in the Second World War, and they were hiding in their little holes. There was no longer a multi-party system. Everything was in the hands of the Communist party 100 percent. Secondly, the forced industrialisation process had prevailed throughout the masses, and bear in mind the fact that Yugoslavia was a country of illiterate and semi-literate people, and when you tell these people that they are going to be an industrial power, and that is what the Communists would say, they forgot about their own republic altogether. Thirdly, in 1948, Stalin declared war on Yugoslavia. This is the well-known conflict between Tito and Stalin. I personally with the army dug trenches on the border with Hungary awaiting for four years an aggression of the Red Army against the former Yugoslavia. This situation created a homogeneous mass which resisted, and then as Stalinism was being destroyed, a new utopia was being created. Instead of the thesis that the Soviet Union is the flowering garden of the new civilisation, the Communist party of Yugoslavia said that the Soviet Union was a dark force, worse than Hitler's Germany. This was the official position of the 6th Congress of the Communist party of Yugoslavia in 1952. They said that a new society would be created based on workers' self-management, and this went on for some 15 years or so. However, then everything changed; namely, if everything is centralised and if, from every republic, every morning aeroplanes go, trains, cars, et cetera, go to the centre; for example, if you want to buy a refrigerator for a hotel, you have to get an import permit from the federal government, and this was the situation until the late '60s. So there was resistance to this kind of centralism within the republicans and this kind of Communist centralism was unbearable. That is one thing. Slovenia and Croatia were permanently bringing pressure to bear with a view to diminishing centralism radically; namely, that the federal government should be a negotiating table where the republics would chart policies.
