On the other hand, there was a contrary phenomenon. The highly centralised state structure appeared as ideal ground for a crawling ideology for great Serbian ideas. Centralism is ideal for this kind of thing, and they thought that it was in this way that they would come to rule Yugoslavia once again in 1962 at a secret meeting on the 12th, 13th, and 14th of March. Tito, at a three-day meeting with about 60 of the top people of Yugoslavia, had a discussion and reached Thesis No. 1. The relations between the republics are such that Yugoslavia was about to break up. Of course, this was a top state secret. Secondly, ideologically, an offensive would have to be waged against centralism and unitarianism. This was in 1962. A new Yugoslav summit was held on the 12th and 13th of November 1965. Bear in mind the fact that the well-known Rankovic was there, he was Vice-President of the republic, the second most important person in Yugoslavia. Also well-known Eduard Kardelj was there. I mean, well-known amongst us. He was the author of all the documents of the Communist party of Yugoslavia and of all the constitutions of Yugoslavia. He came up with the following thesis which is of key importance now. I am quoting him again from memory: We Communists are making a disastrous mistake because with our practical policy we are denying the existence of republics and nations and we cannot continue in this way. When we die, Tito, Kardelj, Rankovic, this guard of the revolution and the war, Yugoslavia will fall into the hands of hegemonist forces; that is, the hegemonist force that is in Serbia. In order to save what we achieved by blood, that is to say, Yugoslavia, through the four years of war that we waged for it, we have to make confederacy out of it, and, if needed, even a federation of sovereign states. That was Kardelj's expose on the 12th and 13th of November, 1965. After that, the pendulum of Yugoslav political life came to move towards confederalism. In 1974, a confederal constitution was adopted which introduced the principle of 100 percent parity and the principle of veto. According to the principle of parity, an Albanian could be the President of the State of Yugoslavia, and this was indeed the case. Fadil Hodza, an Albanian, was President of Yugoslavia because there was a rotating presidency. There were eight federal units, six republics and two autonomous provinces, which were practically made equal by the 1974 constitution. So people from Vojvodina -- Stevan Doronjski, the representative of Vojvodina, more specifically he became President of Yugoslavia, head of state. So this was a semi-confederacy. Some people say confederacy, others don't even say that it was a federation. Some people say there was still a centralist state. No, it was not. But then that's not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a second, Professor. Sorry to interrupt you again. In all these events that you are speaking about, could you tell us briefly what the position of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was at that stage; and in this republic, there were the members of all three nations that are predominant throughout Yugoslavia, namely Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. What is the position of Bosnia in this state, this state that used to be centralist before and now is yielding to the forces of federalism and confederalism?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I know some of this from my own personal experience. I was in government at that time. I didn't have any great political power, but I was near the leaders. You see, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation is quite special because their mainstreams, Serbia and Croatia, acted like a magnet, attracting Serbs from Bosnia to Serbia and Croats from Bosnia to Croatia. For example, in 1921, in Bosnia, 44 percent of the population was Serb, approximately. In 1991, 13 percent less Croats. In 1921 had 23 percent, and in 1991, 17 percent. That is 6 percent less. Muslims in 1921 had about 32 or 33 percent, but in 1991, there was almost 44 percent, 43.7 percent to be more precise. As far as political life is concerned, I must point out a tragic thing. The Croats from Bosnia, notably Herzegovina, who wholeheartedly supported the quisling independent state of Croatia, paid a high price in Bosnia and Herzegovina until the mid '60s. At a party meeting -- I don't know if the gentlemen are aware of these special party meetings, the big ones that were held, that is where big papers were written for -- read out and then research was carried out, and these big meetings would go on for two or three days -- the leader of the Communist party of Bosnia and Herzegovina in May 1965, his name with a Cvijetin Mijatovic, a Serb who was in charge of the Communist party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he said -- after two days of this party meeting on the position of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he said, "I am ashamed as a Serb. I must say that it has been difficult to be a Croat since 1945 until the present day." Let me just add one more thing. Serbs were dominant in Bosnia-Herzegovina because I omitted to mention that Bosnian Serbs and Croatian Serbs were a very strong support of Tito's from 1948 until the end of his life. In terms of percentage, the Serbs of Bosnia and the Serbs of Croatia gave the greatest contribution to Tito's partisan army. However, Bosnia, when the federation became stronger and became more federal, as it were, a group of people came to power in Bosnia, Branko Mikulic, Pozderac, before that Hasam Brkic, and then later some Serbs, the Bosnian state, the Republic of Bosnia, became so self-supporting that it was the most hard-line republic in the negotiations with other republics. And they did not yield. I mean, their leadership did not yield either to Serbia or to Croatia; and according to their political mentality, they somehow accepted that the federal administration would be leading them by the hand. From the '70s onwards, they became a very hard-line republic which defended its interests so strongly, very often clambering against Belgrade and Zagreb and the federal authorities. I said that this was the golden age of Piracles in Bosnia-Herzegovina. From the '70s they started with this expansion, as it were, in terms of infrastructure and modern industry. They created major systems, et cetera, big systems. So they, in a way, became Tito's main support. And, excuse me, but while Belgrade and Zagreb considered that this was a Turkish -- there is an expression, a Turkish dark region as a symbol of backwardness, illiteracy, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, this is the moment to take a break according to the programme that you gave us earlier and then we can continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could finish in about 15 or 20 minutes, so as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. I think that I perhaps made a mistake when I was thinking about today. But I think we will take a 15-minute break anyway. I have noticed that the interpreters do need a break, so we will have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will be only 15, 20 minutes more. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Resumed at 5.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, you mentioned that the rulers of the then Yugoslavia in the '60s at a secret meeting became aware of these disintegration processes that after what seemed firm hegemonism after World War II, these disintegration trends now could be seen. What happened after the state leadership of the former Yugoslavia realised this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: The state leadership, first of all, was divided. A faction of it, led by Tito, Kardelj, Serbian leaders, a part of the leaders of Croatia and Slovenia and so on, as well as a part of the Serbian elite, personally felt that Communism was tying the hands of Serbia. This is paradoxical, but history is a paradox. Let me try to explain that a little bit. People, ordinary people, except extremely privileged ones, kind of looked more towards the West as a democratic society, faith was being lost in Communism, the faith in self-management also was being lost, the country was beginning to be democratised. In 1961, the citizens got passports for the first time, a lot of emigration began, so in 1968-69, there were about 800.000 workers in Germany, in France, in Belgium, in Western Europe as a whole. So that there was pressure from the inside for society to democratise, to open up towards itself from the inside, to be more democratic and also to open up its borders. Yugoslavia was the only Communist state where foreign travel was not banned, and this was a major democratic wave which lasted based on the ideological concept with Soviet Communism. So society was opening up more and more. At the same time, it began to have conflicts amongst the parties on the inside. On one hand, impatient liberals, democrats, wanted even faster democratisation; and then, on the other side, other factions were actually afraid of democratisation, especially the Yugoslav People's Army which was the most indoctrinated Communist institution in the country. Since this democratisation enabled the start of national affirmation, that you could sing national songs, patriotic songs, you could speak more freely about the position of certain nations with Yugoslavia, the army and a part of the war, partisan generation, got afraid, got scared about democratic development. But in spite of that, Tito's authority was extremely powerful. There was no force that could go against him. I said that they had a constitution, new constitution in '74 which was confederal, which is also a paradox. They strengthened the power of the police and the party structure. This was a response to the opposition which was against the constitution in Serbia and also in Croatia. There was the mass pock (phonetic), it was a mass movement in Croatia which shook up Yugoslavia in its own way. I don't know if you want to ask any questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If you permit me, Professor, before you move onto the next topic, mentioning all of these events, you're talking about these internal powers, forces which are acting in the territory of a multi-civilisational, multi-confessional, multi-national state. How does the world view this state, the great powers, because we have seen that since the creation of Yugoslavia, in all of this period that you spoke about, the great powers had a major role. How are they behaving at these times?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was the most extreme, the most hard-core pro-Soviet state in 1945. In Europe, on the whole planet, there was no country which was so loyal to the Soviet Union as Yugoslavia. After 1948, when the conflict happened between Tito and Stalin and when war could have broken out, there was the question of: Where is Yugoslavia going after this conflict? It's lucky for it because at the moment that it left the Soviet bloc -- this was in 1948-1949 -- the NATO pact was treated in 1949 and the Warsaw treaty was created in 1948, even though the Soviet bloc was created in 1948-1949. So it was lucky that Tito brought it out of the Soviet bloc. So then we have the question of whether it will approach the West. It didn't join the West, but it did get military and economic aid from the West. When relations between Khruschev and Tito were normalised, the Soviet Union agreed to Yugoslavia's non-bloc position, the West also said, "Okay, we accept Yugoslavia's non-adherence to blocs." But both blocs, both Super Powers, because Europe was ruled by the Soviet-American peace pacts, so both powers hoped that Yugoslavia one day perhaps will join NATO or turn towards the Warsaw treaty one day. Lucky for Yugoslavia, Tito is one of the leaders of the world's non-aligned movement which comprises over 100 states, Nassar, Nehru, Sukarno, and so on. So that his role as one of the three leading figures of the non-aligned movement was much stronger than Yugoslavia would mean in the world otherwise. So both blocs, the USSR and the USA, made approaches toward Yugoslavia. So Yugoslavia had a privileged position: It didn't belong to any blocs, but both blocs -- how should I say that? -- wanted for it to join them. So Tito played a wonderful, brilliant role. He didn't join one bloc or the other, but this strengthened his position and this strengthened the regime a lot. But Yugoslavia was nevertheless determined by blocs; it could not make major social reforms which would bring it in conflict. Hungary tried to democratise in 1946 and it got tanks, Czechoslovakia tried in 1968 and it got tanks, Berlin tried in 1958 and it got tanks. So the shackles of the Cold War, which shackled all of the countries of Europe, they shackled Yugoslavia too but in a specific way because in a way it became the mascot both of the East and West, and that is one of the factors of its relative stability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In such a situation, in such a specific position that Yugoslavia had its foreign policy aspect; on the other hand, at the outset of the start of the activity of the forces of disintegration that are taking place, how did the great powers react to that? Did they, from their positions, feel that it was better to preserve Yugoslavia as an integral -- or to permit Yugoslavia to disintegrate where events were leading in any case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: I have no proof or arguments based on which I could say that the West wanted destabilisation of Yugoslavia. Quite to the contrary. We had visits from Carter, Kennedy, I don't know who didn't come. Tito went to all the metropolises of the world, so I don't believe that. I believe that the Soviet Union, Breschnev, who several times exerted pressure, he wanted Yugoslavia to enter the East bloc, to leave the position of a non-bloc country, but Tito never permitted that, so that in this aspect, as I said, both blocs in a way agreed to this non-bloc position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Okay. So to bring us to a close. Two processes were parallel towards the end of Tito's life, and the first year after he died, a year before his death, there was a very serious economic crisis in Yugoslavia. The process of industrialisation was stopped and so on. Secondly, based on the confederal constitution of 1974, the state structures of the republics were already so strengthened that they no longer wanted to listen to the federal administration. The federal administration requested more than ordered. But Tito was the absolute master of the situation, absolute, and not one structure, Serbian, Croatian, Slovenia, et cetera, not one of them could do anything without Tito's knowledge. When Tito died, the economic crisis deepened, and now there was the question of whether we could live on without Tito, without his dictatorship which, in my opinion, I thought was positive, but this is where I am subjective, so please don't take this. I am speaking as a former member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party. That's what I was. So let's leave that aside. That's not important. In 1991, there was an uprising by the Albanians in Kosovo. This was a serious matter. The republics agreed to resolve the economic crisis, the serious economic crisis, and there is a conflict among them. Some support public ownership and the market mechanism and the others were saying, "But this is the abandoning of socialism and we won't permit that." After the uprising, the rebellion in Kosovo, Serbia initiates a constitutional process to change the 1974 constitution in two ways: First, the provinces to no longer be members of the federation because they were within the republics so, i.e., for them to be returned into Serbia because before they were autonomous. Second, to limit the powers of the republics in a way that more rights and jurisdiction will be given to the federal administration. Serbia exerts pressure to go into reform. However, according to the constitution in force then, no one can even launch an initiative without a consensus, which means that at the beginning, at the very first step, at the stage of initiative, at the stage of proposing changes, each republic and province has the right to veto. So that all the republics and the provinces unanimously responded to Serbia, "No, no, there are to be no changes, neither in the republics, neither in the provinces. We have to live according to the 1974 constitution, the confederal constitution." This caused a major revolt in Serbia which developed on the basis of old -- what I mentioned in the first part of our conversation. There was a vision created in Serbia that Yugoslavia will break apart, that Croatia and Slovenia will leave Yugoslavia, that if the 1974 constitution is respected, that Serbs in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina will find themselves in a different state if separatism takes place and that Serbia cannot bear such a development. So negotiations between Serbia and the rest of the republics lasted for six years, 1981 to 1987. In the meantime, the temperature in Serbia, the political temperature in Serbia, came to the boiling point. Hundreds of thousands, millions of people came out for meetings with the slogan, "Let's save Yugoslavia. Let's save socialism, Communism." All the republics dug in against reform except Serbia, and Serbia did not have the constitutional ability to change anything. Out of eight members of the federation, it was enough for one to say "No" and there would be no changes; but if all seven say "No," then of course there would be no changes then. Since the temperature had reached a terrible state, the new leadership of Serbia, in 1987, 1988, reached a decision, "We will not negotiate with the rest of Yugo republics. We will bypass the constitution. We will not wait for any negotiations with the other five republics and the provinces. We will go outside the institutional." What does that mean, "outside the institutional"? We will use the argument of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Professor, excuse me for interrupting. When you say the leadership of Serbia comes out with this idea, which leadership is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: The leadership which negotiated for six years, led by Ivan Stombolic (phonetics) was replaced, and a new leadership was formed headed by Slobodan Milosevic in 1987, and this leadership said, "We will not discuss with the republics. We will use force." And then we come to 1987, the fall of Vojvodina, of the autonomy of Vojvodina, the fall of Kosovo in 1988- 1989, and the fall of Montenegro in 1989. When I say "the fall," understand the following: the mass demonstrations, the mobilisation of the population at meetings toppled the leaderships of Vojvodina, Kosovo, and Montenegro. In this way, Milosevic got four votes in the federation: Serbia, Montenegro, Kosovo, and Vojvodina. Now, the balance of power is 4-4 because the new leaderships of Kosovo, Vojvodina, and Montenegro now go hand in hand with Milosevic. On the other side are the other four republics, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Professor. But when you said that the leadership in Vojvodina was replaced and in Kosovo, those were two autonomous provinces with the right to vote in the federal assembly. In order to clarify matters, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how these leaderships were replaced, in what way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: You see, this was a technology (sic) which came to be called "the happening of the people."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was it that happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN BILANDZIC
utterances.text: Party organisations, trade union organisations, various associations, the Serb Orthodox Church, the Association of Writers, different organisations of all kinds, they organised mass rallies that were attended by 100.000, 200.000, 300.000 people. And in 1989, at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers in Belgrade, there were 1 million people. In Kosovo, there were over a million people on the 28th of June, 1989. These rallies were so strong that the leaderships could not sustain this. They simply had to resign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Unfortunately, for reasons which are not up to us, we will have to stop at 6.00. Perhaps now we can adjourn. Let me remind you that we continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 and we were going to work until 2.15 p.m. because we have to coordinate the activities of the two courtrooms. So we shall conclude at this point, Professor, and see you tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
